content.text:
Pulled — canon main is now `a06898a0`, `claudinite-tasks 60831.5`. Two versions landed since my earlier analysis, including [#1503](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1503) eight minutes ago, which touches the janitor.

## Rule B — the agent leash

`janitor-rules.mjs:60`. It is the janitor's answer to a session that died mid-item.

```js
export function deadAgentItems(open = [], now, { leashMs = AGENT_LEASH_MS } = {}) {
  return open.filter((i) => isStatus(i, STATUS_RUNNING_AGENT) && idle(i, now) >= leashMs);
}
```

An item wearing `task:status:running-agent` that has gone **3 hours** without a single update is declared dead. No probe, no liveness check — the rule's own header is explicit that the assumption is *stated rather than discovered*: **"a legitimately longer-running agent must comment on its item to reset the activity clock, or it is declared dead."** The comment it leaves names the session from the hand-off comment, so a human can go read that transcript.

Its purpose is to stop a crashed session holding an item's claim forever. The item would otherwise sit `running-agent` indefinitely, invisible to Rule A (which only looks at `ready`) and to every other rule.

## Why it matters for the 128

Rule B is where the R5 pile comes from, and the reason it can't drain is a two-line collision I want to put side by side. `queue-sweep.mjs:95`:

```js
await escalate(item, deadAgentComment(...), STATUS_RUNNING_AGENT, NEEDS_HUMAN_DECISION);
```

`janitor-rules.mjs:27`:

```js
export const SUPERSEDABLE_PARKS = Object.freeze(['failure', 'action']);
```

Rule B parks **every** dead agent as `decision` — hardcoded, no branch. And `decision` is precisely one of the two kinds Rule E refuses to supersede, for a stated reason: those parks *"carry content a person still owes an answer to,"* and a later success doesn't answer them.

**That reasoning is right for a real decision park and wrong for a Rule B park.** A Rule B park records no human judgment at all — it's the machine noting that a session stopped breathing. It is a *failure*, and `failure` is supersedable. But because it's stamped `decision`, a later clean run of the same task cannot clear it, and it sits forever.

That is the trap that turned one broken `converge-item.mjs` into 91 permanently-parked `decision` items rather than 91 that the next clean run would have swept up.

## So: will the next janitor run fix any?

Answered from the rules on current head, no trigger needed yet:

| kind | count | reachable? |
|---|---|---|
| `decision` | 91 | **No** — excluded from `SUPERSEDABLE_PARKS`; Rule B's own output |
| `approval` | 26 | **No** — excluded too |
| `action` | 11 | **Only these** — supersedable, where a later clean run exists |

Rule G can't help either: it needs `Ends-when: #<n> closed` in the body, which only the post-[#1472](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1472) converge stamps. All 128 predate it.

And [#1503](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1503) just made Rule E *narrower*, deliberately — it now refuses ad-hoc items entirely, because "two verification issues were closed citing a third issue's run, their own `Verify:` assertion never executed."

So the honest answer is **at most 11 of 128, probably fewer.** Triggering the janitor now would be theatre against this backlog. The thing that would actually drain it is making Rule B stamp `failure` — which is both the correct kind and the supersedable one — and that's a canon change, not a sweep.

> ⚠️ Still open: **The 128 parked items** — the janitor cannot reach 117 of them by construction; I have not triggered it, since the rules say it would clear ~11 at best. Say the word and I'll either run it anyway for those 11, or open the Rule B → `failure` fix. **[#1482](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1482)** — diagnosis posted: not an agent bug, a version-collision race between concurrent PRs that a `scope: 'work'` check cannot see; ready for your hand-off. **VascularColoring [#243](https://github.com/missingbulb/VascularColoring/issues/243) / [#242](https://github.com/missingbulb/VascularColoring/issues/242)** — closed `completed`, verified against the vendored mount.

input.title: Rule B parks a dead agent `decision`, the one kind no later run can clear
input.body:
Rule B — the agent leash — declares a session dead after 3h of silence and parks its item. It stamps `task:status:needs-human-decision`, hardcoded, with no branch:

```js
// queue-sweep.mjs:95
await escalate(item, deadAgentComment(...), STATUS_RUNNING_AGENT, NEEDS_HUMAN_DECISION);
```

That is the one park kind a later run can never clear:

```js
// janitor-rules.mjs:27
export const SUPERSEDABLE_PARKS = Object.freeze(['failure', 'action']);
```

Rule E's own reasoning for excluding `decision` is correct **for a decision park** — those *"carry content a person still owes an answer to,"* and a later success does not answer them. It is wrong for a Rule B park, which carries no human judgment at all: it is the machine noting that a session stopped breathing. That is a failure, and `failure` is supersedable.

## What it costs

A single broken `converge-item.mjs` (#1491) left finished runs unable to converge. Rule B's leash caught each of them and parked them `decision`. Because `decision` is unreachable by Rule E, a later clean run of the same task — which is proof the earlier one is no longer broken — cannot clear any of them. They accumulate instead of draining.

The two kinds are also not interchangeable downstream: `failure` is the blocking park (`isBlockingPark`), which holds the task's lane. That is the correct behaviour for a dead session — `instructions.md` already says so for the sibling case, that a convergence which could not be performed *"is the failure park, and never anything else… the failure park is the only one that HOLDS THE TASK'S LANE, and a run that could not converge must stop its task recurring until a person has looked."* Rule B parks exactly that situation and picks the lane-releasing kind, so the task keeps recurring and files a fresh occurrence each anchor.

## The change

Rule B stamps `task:status:needs-human-failure`.

## Also worth deciding, not included here

`statelessItems` (Rule D, `queue-sweep.mjs:121`) stamps `decision` for the same shape of reason — its own comment calls the item *"the leavings of a label swap that tore mid-flight,"* which is breakage, not a choice. Left alone in this change; raising it separately rather than widening the diff.

`scheduler-run.mjs:385` also writes `decision`, and that one is **correct** — it fires only when the task declares `on_interrupt: 'needs-human'`, and it genuinely asks a person to choose ("check whether the interrupted run left anything behind, then re-queue it by hand").

input.title: Rule B parks a dead agent as failure, the kind a later run can clear
input.head: claude/rule-b-parks-failure
input.body:
Closes #1515

Rule B — the agent leash — declares a session dead after 3h of silence and parks its item `task:status:needs-human-decision`, hardcoded. That is the one park kind a later run can never clear:

```js
export const SUPERSEDABLE_PARKS = Object.freeze(['failure', 'action']);
```

Rule E's reasoning for excluding `decision` is right for a real decision park — those *"carry content a person still owes an answer to,"* and a later success does not answer them. It is wrong for a Rule B park, which carries no human judgment at all: it is the machine noting a session stopped breathing. That is a failure, and `failure` is supersedable.

Two consequences both want the same reading:

- **Rule E can now drain them.** A later clean run of the task is proof the earlier one is no longer broken. Under `decision` that proof was inadmissible and the parks accumulated.
- **The lane holds.** `failure` is the blocking park (`isBlockingPark`), so the generator stops filing a fresh occurrence every anchor behind a run nobody has looked at. `instructions.md` already states this for the sibling case — a convergence that could not be performed *"is the failure park, and never anything else… the only one that HOLDS THE TASK'S LANE."* Rule B parks exactly that situation and was picking the lane-releasing kind.

## Assurance

The changed test was watched failing on the old code before the fix (`not ok 2 … expected [needs-human-failure], actual [needs-human-decision]`), and a second test pins the actual invariant rather than the literal — that the kind Rule B parks at is one Rule E can supersede, so this cannot silently regress if either side moves.

876 tests pass in `packs/claudinite-tasks/`. `check_the_work` and `check_the_world` both report 0 blocking.

## Not in this change

`statelessItems` (Rule D, `queue-sweep.mjs:121`) stamps `decision` for the same shape of reason — its own comment calls the item *"the leavings of a label swap that tore mid-flight,"* which is breakage, not a choice. Raised in #1515 rather than widened into this diff.

`scheduler-run.mjs:385` also writes `decision` and is **correct**: it fires only when a task declares `on_interrupt: 'needs-human'`, and genuinely asks a person to choose.

---

## Why convergence didn't run

`converge-item.mjs` calls `api.readIssue`, which does a direct `fetch` to `api.github.com` with `Authorization: Bearer $GITHUB_TOKEN`. In this session, `GITHUB_TOKEN`/`GH_TOKEN` are both a 14-character `proxy-in…` placeholder (the network proxy's own git-credential-rewrite token, not a GitHub API credential) — `api.github.com` returns `401 Bad Credentials` for it. This session's only real GitHub access is the MCP `github` server's tools, which `converge-item.mjs` doesn't use (by design — its own header comment says direct-`GITHUB_TOKEN` REST access is meant for the Action's own environment, "everything session-side stays MCP-only").

Per `queue/instructions.md`: *"If the command refuses... doing it by hand anyway is how an item ends up closed wearing `task:agent`."* I'm taking that literally — not swapping labels or closing the issue myself. This is a needs-human-action situation (a credential/wiring gap in how this project's routine hands work to a Claude Code Web session), not a judgment call for me to paper over.

## What the revalidation found

Scope (per Context): `.claudinite/local/packs` — `browser-speech` and `host-page-adaptation`. Probed every environment-dependent claim in both packs' `RULES.md` against a real, live-launched headless Chromium 141.0.7390.37 (Playwright's bundled build), including loading a minimal MV3 extension to test the content-script/background split. **All nine claims held — nothing was corrected, so no PR.**

**browser-speech/RULES.md**
1. `chrome.tts` is not exposed to content scripts — **HOLDS**. Loaded a minimal MV3 extension (`tts` permission, one content script, one background service worker) against a local http page: `chrome.tts` is `undefined` in the content script (which does see `chrome.runtime`) and defined in the background worker.
2. `webkitSpeechRecognition` owns its capture, no hook for `MediaTrackConstraints` — **HOLDS**. Constructor arity is 0 and no constraint-passing method exists on its prototype chain.
3. Chrome applies its own default AEC to that capture — **UNPROBED**. No real mic/audio pipeline in this sandbox to measure an acoustic effect, and doc lookup was blocked (see below).
4. `suppressLocalAudioPlayback`/`restrictOwnAudio` are `getDisplayMedia`-only and `getUserMedia` "ignores them without a word" — **HOLDS** for the observable half: `getUserMedia({audio:{suppressLocalAudioPlayback:true, restrictOwnAudio:true, ...}})` did not throw or warn (matches "without a word"). The functional half (no real suppression effect on a mic capture) is **UNPROBED**: no hardware to measure it, and doc lookup (MDN) was blocked by this session's network egress policy (`EGRESS_BLOCKED` on `developer.mozilla.org`) — left uncorrected per "unprobed, not disproven" rather than guessed from a fake-device echo.
5. `echoCancellation`/`noiseSuppression`/`autoGainControl` apply only to the capture you own — **HOLDS** (same probe: accepted without error, reflected in `getSettings()`).
6. `SpeechRecognitionPhrase`/`processLocally` gated on Chrome's on-device model — **HOLDS** as far as probed: `processLocally` and static `available()` exist, and `available({langs:["en-US"]})` resolves `"available"` in this build. `phrases`/`SpeechRecognitionPhrase` are absent even after setting `processLocally = true` — but this is Playwright's open-source Chromium, not Google Chrome, and this specific biasing surface is plausibly Chrome-exclusive; correcting the rule off that gap would be exactly this session's own limitation mistaken for the platform's, so left uncorrected and logged as inconclusive.
7. `getVoices()` empty means "not ready yet", lazy via `voiceschanged` — **HOLDS** architecturally (`onvoiceschanged` exists, call is synchronous). The empty→populated transition itself is **UNPROBED**: this headless sandbox has zero TTS voices installed at all, an environment gap rather than a timing question a real Chrome install would show.

**host-page-adaptation/RULES.md**
8. Synthetic `KeyboardEvent` `keyCode`/`which` default to 0 unless the init dict sets them (not derived from `key`) — **HOLDS**, directly probed.
9. Constructed events (`KeyboardEvent`/`MouseEvent`/`CustomEvent`) default `bubbles`/`cancelable`/`composed` to `false` — **HOLDS**, directly probed; underlies the `synthetic-input-events-bubble` check's fix text.

Network egress to `developer.mozilla.org` (and general web domains) is blocked by this session's proxy policy (`EGRESS_BLOCKED`), which is why the two remaining unprobed claims above couldn't be closed out via documentation either — a policy boundary, not something a later pass can fix on its own.

No pack changes: repo working tree is clean, every claim that could be live-probed held, and the two that couldn't were left exactly as written.

CI green (`test-and-conformance`, 84s). Here's the full picture.

## 1. The fix — [PR #1516](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1516), closing [#1515](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1515)

```
packs/claudinite-tasks/tasks/task-janitor/
    Rule B's escalation now stamps needs-human-failure instead of
    needs-human-decision, with the why recorded at the choice site.

packs/claudinite-tasks/
    Version 60831.5 → 60831.6, plus its VERSIONS.md row.
```

I watched the changed test fail on the old code first (`expected [needs-human-failure], actual [needs-human-decision]`). The second test pins the *invariant* rather than the literal — that whatever kind Rule B parks at is one Rule E can supersede — so this can't silently regress if either side moves later. 876 tests pass; `check_the_work` and `check_the_world` both 0 blocking.

Beyond draining, the fix has a second effect worth naming: `failure` is the **blocking** park. Rule B was picking the lane-*releasing* kind, so the generator kept filing a fresh occurrence every anchor behind a run nobody had looked at. That is where the duplicate items came from.

## 2. How many of the 91

The live count is **93** open `decision` parks — 24 canon-spelled, 69 legacy — across 12 repos.

I sampled 5 spanning 5 repos and both label eras. **All 5 are Rule B**, all with the same root cause. Two are worth quoting, because they show the mislabelling directly:

- **TLDR #367** — the agent *finished the work and opened PR #369*, then: *"`converge-item.mjs` … errored with `converge-item: #367 could not be read` … this session's `GITHUB_TOKEN` is not a valid GitHub REST API credential."* It wanted `--outcome approval --pr 369`. Rule B parked it `decision`. **That's an approval wearing a decision label.**
- **Claudinite #1376** — *"Convergence could not run: `converge-item.mjs` failed with `GITHUB_REPOSITORY is not set`."*

Structurally the sample should generalise, because the other writers are nearly ruled out by construction: Rule D only fires on items with *no* status label; `scheduler-run` only on tasks declaring `on_interrupt: 'needs-human'`; and an agent-*chosen* `decision` required `converge-item.mjs` to work — which is exactly what was broken. **So ~86 of the 93 are Rule B**, with the 7 `Verify in production:` ad-hoc items the plausible exceptions.

## 3. What else closes as `decision` — and yes, the label is the problem

Three machine writers, and they do not mean the same thing:

| site | fires when | is it really a decision? |
|---|---|---|
| `queue-sweep.mjs:95` — **Rule B** | agent silent 3h | **No** — machine found a corpse. *Fixed in #1516.* |
| `queue-sweep.mjs:121` — **Rule D** | item has no status label at all | **No** — its own comment calls it *"the leavings of a label swap that tore mid-flight"*. That's breakage. |
| `scheduler-run.mjs:385` | executor silent **and** task declares `on_interrupt: 'needs-human'` | **Yes** — genuinely asks a person to choose whether the interrupted run left anything behind. |

Your instinct is right, and I'd put the diagnosis more sharply than "unclear naming": **`decision` has become the default sink for "the machine doesn't know what happened."** Two of its three automatic writers use it to mean *broken*, which is what `failure` is for — and because `decision` is the kind Rule E may never clear, every mislabelling is permanent. The vocabulary's real axis isn't four peer kinds; it's one binary (*does this hold the task's lane?*) with a reason attached, and `decision` currently straddles it.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files and comment-only changes.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

input.title: The janitor stops writing `decision`: rules B and D park failure
input.body:
Closes #1515

Two janitor rules stamped `task:status:needs-human-decision` for situations no human decided. That is the one park kind a later run can never clear:

```js
export const SUPERSEDABLE_PARKS = Object.freeze(['failure', 'action']);
```

input.body:
#1516 fixed two writers that put machine observations into `needs-human-decision`. That was the bug. This is the design question underneath it: the vocabulary made those writers easy to get wrong, and one of them was wrong from the day it was written.

## The four kinds encode two things at once

| kind | what it says the human owes | holds the lane? |
|---|---|---|
| `failure` | read the trace, something broke | **yes** |
| `action` | change something outside the code | no |
| `decision` | choose what happens next | no |
| `approval` | merge or close a PR | no |

Two independent axes are collapsed into one label:

1. **Does this hold the task's lane?** A mechanical property with exactly one correct answer per situation, and real consequences — the generator files no further occurrence while a blocking park stands.
2. **What is a person being asked for?** Routing information for whoever reads the queue.

They are genuinely independent. A dead session both holds the lane *and* asks someone to read a trace. An approval releases the lane and asks for a merge. Nothing about the second axis determines the first, yet one label carries both, so choosing a kind means silently deciding a scheduling question while thinking about a human-facing one.

That is what went wrong in #1515: rules B and D each picked the right *description* — "someone needs to look at this and decide" — and thereby picked the wrong *scheduling behaviour*, releasing a lane that should have held. The description was even defensible in isolation. Only the coupling made it a bug.

## `decision` is the default sink

Its definition is the only one phrased as a residual — "you stopped mid-flight and what happens next is a choice." Every kind's definition names a specific remedy except this one, which names the absence of one. Predictably it collects everything that does not obviously fit, and it is the kind rule E can never clear, so whatever lands there stays. 93 items across the fleet are sitting in it right now.

Note also that `instructions.md` already tells the *agent* that `failure` is the fallback: *"Use this when you are unsure."* Two different defaults for the same taxonomy — `failure` for a session, `decision` in practice for the janitor's own code — is itself evidence the vocabulary is not carrying its meaning.

## Options

**A. Separate the axes.** A park becomes a blocking flag plus a reason. The mechanical question is answered explicitly at each write site instead of as a side effect of naming a remedy. Costs a label-shape migration across every member.

**B. Re-cut the kinds so each names a remedy.** Retire `decision` as a distinct kind; anything currently landing there is either a failure (something broke), an action (something outside the code must change), or an approval (an artifact is waiting). Smallest conceptual change, but leans on the claim that every real park genuinely is one of the other three — which wants testing against the 93 before anyone commits to it.

**C. Keep the four, fix the defaults.** State the lane consequence in each kind's definition, make `failure` the documented fallback everywhere, and add a check that a machine writer never stamps `decision`. Cheapest, and #1516 already does the last part by hand; it leaves the coupling in place.

I have not picked one. **B looks most promising and is the one I would test first**, but the evidence that would settle it is the same investigation now running over the 93 parked items — what each one *actually* was. That should land before this is decided.

## What is already true

- #1516 — rules B and D park `failure`; the janitor writes no `decision` at all.
- `scheduler-run.mjs:385` still writes `decision` and is correct: it fires only for `on_interrupt: 'needs-human'` and genuinely asks a person to choose. Any re-cut has to keep somewhere for that case to live.

## How many of the 91 are Rule B

The current fleet count is **93** open `decision` parks — 24 canon-spelled, 69 legacy — spread over 13 repos.

I sampled five, across five repos and both label eras. **All five were Rule B**, carrying its exact signature comment, and the threads name the cause in the agent's own words:

- Claudinite [#1376](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1376) — *"`converge-item.mjs` failed with `GITHUB_REPOSITORY is not set`"*
- TLDR [#367](https://github.com/missingbulb/TLDR/issues/367) — work finished, PR #369 open, wanted `--outcome approval --pr 369`, couldn't converge. **Parked `decision` by the leash.** That one is an approval wearing the wrong label entirely.

The structural argument says the sample generalises. Only three writers stamp `decision`, and two are now ruled out for these items: Rule D requires *no* status label (all 93 have one), and `scheduler-run.mjs` fires only for `on_interrupt: 'needs-human'` — which is `implement-request`, i.e. only the seven `Verify in production:` items. The fourth writer is the agent choosing `decision` via `converge-item.mjs` — and `converge-item.mjs` was broken, so no agent could choose anything.

**So ~86 of 93 are Rule B, with at most 7 legitimately the scheduler's.** I'll confirm exactly in the investigation.

## What else writes `decision`

| writer | verdict |
|---|---|
| Rule B — dead agent | **was wrong**, fixed |
| Rule D — stateless repair | **was wrong**, fixed (your call) |
| `scheduler-run.mjs:385` — interrupted `on_interrupt: 'needs-human'` | **correct** — genuinely asks a person to choose |
| an agent's own `converge --outcome decision` | correct by construction |

The janitor now writes **no `decision` park at all**. Every kind it stamps is something the machine observed — which is the only thing an unattended sweep is in a position to assert.

## On the label

You're right that it isn't clear enough, and I think the specific defect is sharper than vagueness — filed as [#1538](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1538). One label carries two independent things: *does this hold the task's lane* (mechanical, one right answer, real scheduling consequence) and *what does a person owe* (routing). Rules B and D each picked a defensible description and thereby silently picked the wrong scheduling behaviour. Only the coupling made that a bug.

`decision` is also the only kind defined as a residual — every other names a remedy, it names the absence of one — so it collects the leftovers, and it's the kind Rule E can never clear. The telling detail: `instructions.md` already tells *agents* that `failure` is the fallback when unsure, so the taxonomy has two different defaults depending on who's writing.

I laid out three options and did **not** pick one. Option B (retire `decision`, since every real park is arguably a failure, action, or approval) looks best, but the evidence that settles it is the same investigation into what those 93 actually were. That should land first.

> ⚠️ Still open: **[PR #1516](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1516)** — CI in progress; 882 tests and both check scopes clean locally. Watch for the version number: main claimed `60831.6` **and** `.7` while I held `.6`, so I rebased to `.8` — that's #1482's race, caught only because the numbers differed. **The 93 parked items** — investigating what each actually was, per your choice; nothing relabelled yet. **[#1538](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1538)** — park vocabulary; proposal deliberately waits on that investigation. **[#1482](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1482)** — diagnosis posted, still yours to hand off, and it just reproduced live in this branch.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files and comment-only changes.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

# Verify in production

A change is finished when someone has watched it work. Most changes you can watch **now**, and
that is the rule — this skill is only for the rest: a change whose proof lives somewhere the
repo cannot see yet. You are filing the proof, not doing the work — and the proof itself runs
unattended: an automatic check, end to end, with a person entering
only where no automatic check can exist.

## When it fires: after the merge, never before

**The PR must have merged.** This skill runs as a step of the merge, unasked — `merge-to-main`
calls it once the squash has landed — and at no other moment. Not when the code is written, not
when the PR opens, not while review is in flight.

The reason is that a PR can be **rejected**, and a branch that is still open can be rewritten
under you. Both leave a verification whose premise never reached `main`:

- A **rewritten branch** makes the brief describe a change that no longer exists. #1121 was filed
  against a scope its PR then dropped; the verification was moot before the merge it waited on.
- A **rejected PR** is worse, because the queue cannot tell it from a merge. A blocked item
  releases on its blocker being *closed*, and nothing reads `merged` — so the item goes ready,
  reads an `In-production-when:` that can never become true, pushes `Not-before:` forward by
  `Retry-every:` without comment, and repeats indefinitely. No janitor rule reclaims it: the
  stale-ready sweep cannot see an item sleeping on a future `Not-before`, and the
  stuck-dependency sweep exempts an item whose blockers have closed.

So there is no such thing as filing this early and letting the queue sort it out. Wait for the
merge, then read **what actually landed** — the merged diff, not the branch you remember writing.

## First: does this file anything at all?

Most changes **file nothing.** Run the test in this order and stop at the first answer:

1. **Did you watch it work in this session?** Then it is proven. File nothing.
2. **Did a test that ran prove it?** A unit test, a CI job, an executable-requirements or UI
   test covering exactly the behaviour that changed. File nothing — the suite is the mechanism
   that comes back.
3. **Does the change have an observable effect at all?** A comment, a design doc, a README, a
   rename with no behavioural edge, a refactor a passing suite already pins. File nothing.
4. **Otherwise: where does its effect first become observable?** If the answer is a place and a
   moment — a member repo once it converges, a site once it deploys, a session once it reloads
   its rules — that is what you file.

The bar is *could not be watched now*, not *would be nice to double-check*. A verification
filed for a change already covered by a test is a wasted run re-proving what the suite proved.

## What you file

**A deferred request** — the same ad-hoc lane `/do-later` rides, so the queue does the waiting,
the running and the lifecycle; nothing here adds machinery beside it. One issue, titled
`Verify in production: <the change, in a few words>`, its body the whole brief: the run that
verifies will never see this conversation and may be days away. Say what changed and why it
could not be watched now, then, each spelled verbatim on its own line:

```
Original-issue: #<the change's issue>
In-production-when: <the concrete artifact to read, and what makes it true>
Verify: <what to observe, and what counts as a pass>
Not-before: <ISO instant just past the expected release>
Retry-every: <how far to push Not-before when not yet live, e.g. 1 day>
```

No `Blocked-by:`. You are filing after the merge, so the change's PR has already closed and
there is nothing left to wait on but the release itself.

- **`Original-issue:`** is where a failure lands — the issue the change was done under, which
  the run reopens if the verification fails. Make the verification that issue's **sub-issue**
  too (`mcp__github__sub_issue_write`, method `add`, `issue_number` the original,
  `sub_issue_id` the **id** the create call returned, not its number), so the change it proves
  shows what is still unproven about it — [RULES.md](../../RULES.md)' *Filing an issue that
  belongs under another*, applied where there is no PR left to carry the link.
- **`In-production-when:`** names a thing to *read*, never a duration to wait. "`missingbulb/Shepherd`'s
  `.claudinite-settings.json` stamps `packVersions.tidy-repo` at 8 or higher." "The live site's
  `/version.json` reports a version past 4.2.0." "Any session started after this landed — check
  the vendored copy under `.claudinite/shared/` carries the new text." A merge is not a
  production condition, and neither is elapsed time.
- **`Verify:`** is an assertion with a pass condition, not a topic — and a read an **unattended
  run can make**: an API response, a file at a URL, an issue's state. "Issue #100 on that repo
  is closed with a comment citing the scheduler runs" beats "check tidy-issues works". Only where no
  automatic check can exist may `Verify:` name a person's step, spelled out exactly.
- **`Not-before:`** is the queue's own wait field: adoption holds the run until the moment has
  passed. Aim it just past the release you expect — the re-arm covers a miss, so don't pad it.
- **`Retry-every:`** is the extension you are prescribing: when the run finds the change not
  yet live, it pushes `Not-before:` forward by exactly this much. Size it to the release you
  wait on — a nightly converge retries daily, a next-session rule in minutes.

Then the mark, as `/do-later` applies it: **`task:origin:ad-hoc`**, the one label the scheduler
run adopts. Beside it, in the body, **`Model: sonnet`** (reading a live artifact and judging an
assertion against it). Never `Automerge:` — a verification has nothing to merge. If the mark
doesn't exist in the repo yet, say so and leave the issue — it appears on the next scheduler run.

## Tell the run how to converge

End the body with instructions to the run itself — the issue is its whole brief, and the run
decides nothing: it executes this playbook.

1. Read `In-production-when:` against the real artifact. Never infer it from a merge, a green
   run, or elapsed time.
2. **Live** → run `Verify:`. Passes: comment the evidence actually read (the version, the value,
   the URL) and close this issue as completed. Fails: reopen `Original-issue:` with a comment
   saying what was asserted, what happened instead and where you read it; comment here linking
   that; close this issue as completed — the verification did its job by finding the fault.
3. **Not yet live** → push `Not-before:` forward by `Retry-every:`, **clear the issue's
   `task:status:*` label** (clearing the status is the whole of the re-ask — the mark stays on
   for life), and leave the issue open. The next scheduler run re-adopts it, and the bumped
   field holds it until the new moment. No comment; the bumped field is the record.

## Then say what you filed

One line back to the owner: the issue link, what it waits on, and its retry cadence.

skills.content:
Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Shepherd/.claude/skills/verify-in-production

# Verify in production

A change is finished when someone has watched it work. Most changes you can watch **now**, and
that is the rule — this skill is only for the rest: a change whose proof lives somewhere the
repo cannot see yet. You are filing the proof, not doing the work — and the proof itself runs
unattended: an automatic check, end to end, with a person entering
only where no automatic check can exist.

## When it fires: after the merge, never before

**The PR must have merged.** This skill runs as a step of the merge, unasked — `merge-to-main`
calls it once the squash has landed — and at no other moment. Not when the code is written, not
when the PR opens, not while review is in flight.

The reason is that a PR can be **rejected**, and a branch that is still open can be rewritten
under you. Both leave a verification whose premise never reached `main`:

- A **rewritten branch** makes the brief describe a change that no longer exists. #1121 was filed
  against a scope its PR then dropped; the verification was moot before the merge it waited on.
- A **rejected PR** is worse, because the queue cannot tell it from a merge. A blocked item
  releases on its blocker being *closed*, and nothing reads `merged` — so the item goes ready,
  reads an `In-production-when:` that can never become true, pushes `Not-before:` forward by
  `Retry-every:` without comment, and repeats indefinitely. No janitor rule reclaims it: the
  stale-ready sweep cannot see an item sleeping on a future `Not-before`, and the
  stuck-dependency sweep exempts an item whose blockers have closed.

So there is no such thing as filing this early and letting the queue sort it out. Wait for the
merge, then read **what actually landed** — the merged diff, not the branch you remember writing.

## First: does this file anything at all?

Most changes **file nothing.** Run the test in this order and stop at the first answer:

1. **Did you watch it work in this session?** Then it is proven. File nothing.
2. **Did a test that ran prove it?** A unit test, a CI job, an executable-requirements or UI
   test covering exactly the behaviour that changed. File nothing — the suite is the mechanism
   that comes back.
3. **Does the change have an observable effect at all?** A comment, a design doc, a README, a
   rename with no behavioural edge, a refactor a passing suite already pins. File nothing.
4. **Otherwise: where does its effect first become observable?** If the answer is a place and a
   moment — a member repo once it converges, a site once it deploys, a session once it reloads
   its rules — that is what you file.

The bar is *could not be watched now*, not *would be nice to double-check*. A verification
filed for a change already covered by a test is a wasted run re-proving what the suite proved.

## What you file

**A deferred request** — the same ad-hoc lane `/do-later` rides, so the queue does the waiting,
the running and the lifecycle; nothing here adds machinery beside it. One issue, titled
`Verify in production: <the change, in a few words>`, its body the whole brief: the run that
verifies will never see this conversation and may be days away. Say what changed and why it
could not be watched now, then, each spelled verbatim on its own line:

```
Original-issue: #<the change's issue>
In-production-when: <the concrete artifact to read, and what makes it true>
Verify: <what to observe, and what counts as a pass>
Not-before: <ISO instant just past the expected release>
Retry-every: <how far to push Not-before when not yet live, e.g. 1 day>
```

No `Blocked-by:`. You are filing after the merge, so the change's PR has already closed and
there is nothing left to wait on but the release itself.

- **`Original-issue:`** is where a failure lands — the issue the change was done under, which
  the run reopens if the verification fails. Make the verification that issue's **sub-issue**
  too (`mcp__github__sub_issue_write`, method `add`, `issue_number` the original,
  `sub_issue_id` the **id** the create call returned, not its number), so the change it proves
  shows what is still unproven about it — [RULES.md](../../RULES.md)' *Filing an issue that
  belongs under another*, applied where there is no PR left to carry the link.
- **`In-production-when:`** names a thing to *read*, never a duration to wait. "`missingbulb/Shepherd`'s
  `.claudinite-settings.json` stamps `packVersions.tidy-repo` at 8 or higher." "The live site's
  `/version.json` reports a version past 4.2.0." "Any session started after this landed — check
  the vendored copy under `.claudinite/shared/` carries the new text." A merge is not a
  production condition, and neither is elapsed time.
- **`Verify:`** is an assertion with a pass condition, not a topic — and a read an **unattended
  run can make**: an API response, a file at a URL, an issue's state. "Issue #100 on that repo
  is closed with a comment citing the scheduler runs" beats "check tidy-issues works". Only where no
  automatic check can exist may `Verify:` name a person's step, spelled out exactly.
- **`Not-before:`** is the queue's own wait field: adoption holds the run until the moment has
  passed. Aim it just past the release you expect — the re-arm covers a miss, so don't pad it.
- **`Retry-every:`** is the extension you are prescribing: when the run finds the change not
  yet live, it pushes `Not-before:` forward by exactly this much. Size it to the release you
  wait on — a nightly converge retries daily, a next-session rule in minutes.

Then the mark, as `/do-later` applies it: **`task:origin:ad-hoc`**, the one label the scheduler
run adopts. Beside it, in the body, **`Model: sonnet`** (reading a live artifact and judging an
assertion against it). Never `Automerge:` — a verification has nothing to merge. If the mark
doesn't exist in the repo yet, say so and leave the issue — it appears on the next scheduler run.

## Tell the run how to converge

End the body with instructions to the run itself — the issue is its whole brief, and the run
decides nothing: it executes this playbook.

1. Read `In-production-when:` against the real artifact. Never infer it from a merge, a green
   run, or elapsed time.
2. **Live** → run `Verify:`. Passes: comment the evidence actually read (the version, the value,
   the URL) and close this issue as completed. Fails: reopen `Original-issue:` with a comment
   saying what was asserted, what happened instead and where you read it; comment here linking
   that; close this issue as completed — the verification did its job by finding the fault.
3. **Not yet live** → push `Not-before:` forward by `Retry-every:`, **clear the issue's
   `task:status:*` label** (clearing the status is the whole of the re-ask — the mark stays on
   for life), and leave the issue open. The next scheduler run re-adopts it, and the bumped
   field holds it until the new moment. No comment; the bumped field is the record.

## Then say what you filed

One line back to the owner: the issue link, what it waits on, and its retry cadence.

# Merge to main

If the project's own `CLAUDE.md` names a merge-policy file, that file overrides the divergent
points below (merge method, CI gating). Don't go hunting for one it doesn't name.

1. Load `create_pull_request` + `merge_pull_request` in one `ToolSearch`.
2. No PR open for the branch? `create_pull_request` (base `main`), body ending `Closes #<issue>`.
3. If the PR has check runs, wait for them to pass. None — merge without waiting.
4. `merge_pull_request`, `merge_method: squash`, title `<subject> (#<pr>)`. Don't pre-read
   mergeability; the call fails loudly.
5. Sync local `main`: `git checkout main && git pull origin main`.
6. Capture the conversation:
   `node .claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`
   (in the canon repo: `node packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`). Skip only if
   the repo doesn't declare `claudinite-growth`. A later merge in the same session runs it again.
7. Run the basics pack's
   [verify-in-production](../../../basics/skills/verify-in-production/SKILL.md) skill, unasked.
   This step is that skill's **only** trigger — it files against what the squash actually landed,
   which is why it runs here and not when the code was written or the PR opened. It decides
   whether this change needs a production check at all — most don't — and files the issue that
   comes back once the change is live. Never offer the owner to check later instead.

Don't re-read the issue to confirm it closed — `Closes #<issue>` does that on merge.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. content.text:
**365 open issues across 16 repos** — 162 queue-managed, 203 plain. The `decision` question is now settled by evidence rather than inference, and it changed my answer.

## Fleet totals

| | Count |
|---|---:|
| Queue items (`task:*` labelled) | **162** |
| — parked awaiting a human | **145** |
| — blocked / waiting / unlabelled | 17 |
| Plain issues | **203** |

## Parks by kind and label generation

| Kind | Legacy vocab | Canon vocab | Total | What it means |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| **decision** | 64 | 29 | **93** | 88 are janitor mislabels — see below |
| **approval** | 12 | 18 | **30** | Genuine: a PR waiting on you |
| **action** | 13 | 5 | **18** | Genuine: a human step required |
| **failure** | 2 | 2 | **4** | Genuine breakage |
| | | | **145** | |

91 of 162 queue items still carry the **retired** `needs-human` + `task:needs-human-*` spelling — they were parked before the rename and no flow re-labels an already-parked item, so they sit outside the canon vocabulary the dashboard and janitor read.

## The 93 decision parks — verified, not estimated

I sampled all three cohorts instead of trusting the structural argument, and the structural argument was **wrong in one place**.

| Cause | Count | Evidence |
|---|---:|---|
| **Rule B** — dead agent leash | **88** | Shepherd [#338](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/issues/338) carries the leash comment verbatim: *"carried `task:status:running-agent` for over 3h with no activity"*. MissingBulbWebsite [#237](https://github.com/missingbulb/MissingBulbWebsite/issues/237) the same in legacy phrasing. |
| **Genuine agent-chosen decision** | **5** | The `claudinite-lifecycle/update` cluster from today. |

My earlier reasoning was that agents *can't* write `decision` because `converge-item.mjs` can't run session-side. That's true of the script but **not** of the outcome: agents replicate the transition by hand over MCP — the path this repo's own rules prescribe. VascularColoring [#314](https://github.com/missingbulb/VascularColoring/issues/314) and LaughCounter [#357](https://github.com/missingbulb/LaughCounter/issues/357) both post a correct `claudinite-task-exec … failed` record and hold an open PR. Those five are real decisions, correctly labelled.

Two things fall out that I hadn't seen before:

**The 5 are one decision, not five.** Every `update` run hit the same staged `.claudinite/pending-workflows/claudinite-executor.yml`, and the two agents I read reached *opposite* readings of the same canon text — #314 called it a canon bug to park; #357 called `task.md` §2 and `VERSIONS.md` 60831.1 directly contradictory and refused to guess. Five open PRs are waiting on one call about a contradiction in canon.

**`decision` is the one kind that can neither self-clear nor hold its lane.** `isBlockingPark` is `failure` only; `SUPERSEDABLE_PARKS` is `['failure','action']`. So a decision park can't be superseded by a later clean run *and* doesn't stop the generator re-filing the same task. That's the accumulation engine: **30 of the 93 are redundant re-filings of a lane already parked** — `Claudinite/tidy-repo/tidy-issues` alone has five open copies (#1376, #1365, #1307, #1201, #1146). 63 distinct lanes, 93 issues.

That is the concrete cost of the bug I merged the fix for. It also means the fix alone drains nothing: the 88 stay `decision` forever unless relabelled to `failure`, at which point Rule E clears them automatically on each task's next clean run.

## One inconsistency my fix introduced

Worth feeding to [#1538](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1538) before it's decided: the same event — a silent run — now parks at **`failure`** when the janitor catches the agent lane, but still at **`decision`** when the scheduler catches the executor lane (`scheduler-run.mjs:385`, gated on `on_interrupt: 'needs-human'`, which exactly one task declares: `implement-request`, the task every ad-hoc item runs). ClaudiniteWebsite #288/#285/#255 sit in that ambiguous zone. I did not touch that writer — it was outside #1515's scope — but the vocabulary decision should cover both or the split just moves.

## Plain issues (203)

| Category | Count |
|---|---:|
| Unlabelled backlog | 59 |
| `quick-win` | 36 |
| `needs-decision` | 29 |
| Tidy trackers | 27 |
| `blocked` | 21 |
| Schedule boards | 14 |
| `add-packs` | 6 |
| `claude-queued` | 4 |
| `workflow-failure` | 4 |
| `plan-tracking` / other | 3 |

Two clusters stand out. **Seven repos hold a duplicate issue for the same converge-item dead end** — MissingBulbWebsite #227, CrosswordChat #304, ClaudiniteWebsite #274 and #277, ClaudiniteCanary #239, EdFringeNow #482, WIP #62 — filed independently by seven sessions each rediscovering it. And **four `workflow-failure` issues are still open** (TLDR #94/#93 from 2026-07-13, ClaudiniteWebsite #204, EdFringeNow #401), alongside MissingBulbWebsite #217 reporting its scheduler frozen since 2026-08-21 — that repo may not be running tasks at all.

The complete 365-issue listing is in the file above, split into Part A (queue) and Part B (plain), grouped by repo with status and label generation per row.

> ⚠️ Still open — nothing acted on this run, per your "investigate before acting": **The 88 Rule B parks** need a one-time relabel `decision` → `failure` to become self-clearing; 30 of them are duplicate lanes that could close outright. Say the word and I'll do it. **The 5 `update` parks** ([VascularColoring #314](https://github.com/missingbulb/VascularColoring/issues/314), [hitbut #173](https://github.com/missingbulb/hitbut/issues/173), [TLDR #422](https://github.com/missingbulb/TLDR/issues/422), [ClaudiniteCanary #309](https://github.com/missingbulb/ClaudiniteCanary/issues/309), [LaughCounter #357](https://github.com/missingbulb/LaughCounter/issues/357)) are five open PRs waiting on one call about a `task.md` §2 vs `VERSIONS.md` 60831.1 contradiction — that one is genuinely yours. **[#1538](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1538)** now has its deciding evidence, plus the scheduler/janitor split above. **91 queue items** still on retired label spellings. **[#1482](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1482)** still awaiting your hand-off.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files and comment-only changes.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.

- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.

Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.

name: single-issue-triage
description: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
---

# Single-issue triage

Triage **one** open issue and take the **first** applicable action. This **acts** — but every action
defaults to the reversible option when the check is inconclusive.

- **Already implemented in `main`** → **close** (`completed`) + a one-line comment citing where it
  landed.
- **Conflicts with a current guideline** → label `needs-decision` + a comment naming the conflict.
- **Blocked by another issue** → label `blocked` + a comment `blocked by #N`.
- **Small and quick to do** → label `quick-win` + a comment scoping it.
- **Else** → leave it.

**Every checkbox in the issue body ticked** is the author's own claim that the work is done — the
strongest completion signal an issue can carry, and the one thing that puts an otherwise quiet issue
into the first rung. It is **a claim, not proof**: read it as a reason to run the implemented-in-`main`
check, never as the answer. Verified ⇒ close; not ⇒ comment naming what is still missing. A
partially-ticked list is not a completion signal at all — triage the issue as if it carried no boxes.
Where the ask has **no repo-side artifact** (a console setting, a routine only a human can touch), those
ticks by the issue's own author are the closing condition — say so and close.

**"Implemented in `main`" means the issue's actual ask is true of `main`'s content _now_** — confirm
it there and cite it. **Never** infer it from a linked PR merging or the issue merely looking done. If
you can't point to it, **comment, don't close.** Create a label if it's missing. Return `{ action,
note }` (action one of closed/needs-decision/blocked/quick-win/left/unchanged).

input.title: A skill for the fleet-wide issue and task triage report
input.body:
Today's triage run — 365 open issues across the 16-repo fleet, 162 of them queue items — was assembled by hand: sixteen `list_issues` calls transcribed into a TSV, a throwaway classifier, and a sampling pass to attribute causes. The analysis was worth having (it found that 88 of 93 `decision` parks were janitor Rule B mislabels, that 30 of them are redundant re-filings of an already-parked lane, and that `decision` is the one park kind that neither holds its lane nor can be superseded), but none of the method survived the session.

Land it as a skill in the `shepherd` local pack so the next run starts from the method instead of rediscovering it.

What the skill has to carry:

- **Collection** — the roster from `list_repos`, one `list_issues` per repo with the field subset and the label/state filter that keep it under the token cap, and the traps this repo has already paid for (`search_issues`'s unreliable title filtering, `minimal_output` not bounding a response on its own).
- **Classification** — queue items vs plain issues, park kind, label generation (canon `task:status:*` vs retired `needs-human` pair), and lane duplication. Suggested as a starting set, not a fixed one: each run should find the categorisation that makes *this* fleet state legible.
- **Cause attribution** — the discriminators that let a run say *why* an item is parked rather than guess: who can write each park kind, what the janitor's rule comments read like verbatim, and the timestamp-clustering signal that separates a fleet-wide sweep from scattered agent work.
- **The standing rule that a structural argument must be sampled before it is reported.** Today's structural case for "no agent can write `decision`" was sound about `converge-item.mjs` and still wrong, because agents replicate the transition by hand over MCP. One sampled comment thread overturned it.

Assessment only — the skill reports, it never relabels or closes.

mkdir -p .claudinite/local/packs/shepherd/skills/fleet-triage && cat > .claudinite/local/packs/shepherd/skills/fleet-triage/SKILL.md <<'SKILLEOF'
---
name: fleet-triage
description: Survey every open issue across the whole missingbulb fleet, split the queue items from the plain ones, and attribute each parked task to the cause that actually parked it. Use when asked for a triage run, a fleet overview, a stuck-tasks analysis, or "all open issues across the fleet".
---

# Fleet triage

A standing survey of every open issue in the fleet, and a cause-level read of the queue items
among them. It **assesses and reports** — it never relabels, closes, or re-queues. Acting on what
it finds is a separate, separately-approved change.

The report has two halves, and the second is the one worth the run:

1. **Every open issue**, categorised — the complete picture, so nothing is invisible.
2. **The queue items, attributed** — not *what state is this in* (the label already says that) but
   *what put it there*, which the label frequently gets wrong.

## The one rule that makes it worth reading

**A structural argument is a hypothesis until you have sampled it.** Reason from the code about
what *can* produce a state, then read at least one real item per cohort before reporting any of it.

This is not caution for its own sake — it is the rule this skill exists because of. A previous run
proved from canon that no agent could write a `decision` park (`converge-item.mjs` cannot reach the
GitHub API session-side, so the outcome path is dead) and reported ~86 of 93 as machine mislabels.
The reasoning about the *script* was correct and the conclusion was still wrong: agents replicate
that transition **by hand over the GitHub MCP tools**, which is the path this repo's own rules
prescribe. One sampled comment thread overturned it. Sample every cohort you intend to name.

## 1. Collect

The roster comes from `mcp__Claude_Code_Remote__list_repos` (query `missingbulb`). Drop archived
repos and anything in `exclude` on the `claudinite-fleet-sheepdog` config in
`.claudinite-settings.json` — that key is the fleet's only opt-out.

Then **one `mcp__github__list_issues` per repo**, and shape the call so it survives:

```
state: "OPEN", perPage: 100, fields: ["number","title","labels","updated_at"]
```

Omitting `body` is what keeps a 99-issue repo under the token cap. Cross-check each response's
`totalCount` against the rows you got, and reconcile the sum before analysing anything.

Do **not** enumerate with `mcp__github__search_issues` — RULES.md records why its query filtering
cannot be trusted, on either search tool, and an unfiltered result overflows. `list_issues` per
repo, with the field subset, is the reliable path. If a repo is not attached, `add_repo` it;
never report a repo as unreachable without checking `list_repos` first.

**Write the rows to a TSV in the scratchpad and classify with a script.** Sixteen repos of labels
is past what eyeballing gets right, and a script makes every count reproducible and every
recategorisation free — you will want to re-cut the data two or three times before the interesting
axis appears.

## 2. Split queue items from plain issues

An issue is **queue-managed** if its title starts `[claudinite-work]`, or it carries any `task:`
label, or the retired `needs-human` / `origin:schedule` marks. Everything else is a plain issue.
Both halves belong in the report; they answer different questions.

Note the **label generation** on every queue item: canon `task:status:*` versus the retired
`needs-human` + `task:needs-human-*` pair. Nothing re-labels an already-parked item, so the
generation is a rough clock — and a large legacy population is itself a finding, because those
items sit outside the vocabulary the janitor and dashboard read.

## 3. Categorise — suggestions, not a fixed set

Start from these axes, then **find the cut that makes this particular fleet state legible.** A run
that only reproduces the axes below has under-delivered; each run should surface at least one
grouping the list does not name.

- **Park kind** — `failure`, `action`, `decision`, `approval`.
- **Label generation** — canon vs retired.
- **Lane duplication** — group by `(repo, pack/task)`. More than one open park on a lane means the
  generator kept re-filing behind a park that never held it. Report distinct lanes alongside the
  raw count; the gap is the redundancy.
- **Non-park queue states** — `blocked`, `waiting-for-executor`, bare `needs-human` with no kind,
  and items with no status label at all (a torn label swap).
- **Cross-repo duplicates** — the same defect filed independently in many repos is a signal about
  the *fleet*, not the repos. Seven separate issues for one converge-item dead end said more than
  any of them did alone.
- **Plain issues** — `quick-win`, `needs-decision`, `blocked`, tidy trackers, schedule boards,
  `add-packs`, `workflow-failure`, unlabelled backlog. An open `workflow-failure`, or a repo
  reporting its own scheduler frozen, means that member may not be running tasks at all — chase
  that before tallying anything else about it.

Other cuts worth trying when the data suggests them: age of the park, whether an open PR is
attached (a park holding a finished PR is a different problem from a park holding nothing), which
task dominates, and which repos are contributing disproportionately.

## 4. Attribute cause

**Derive the writers from canon rather than trusting any table — including this one.** The park
vocabulary is under active change, so read it fresh each run, from a current checkout:

```
grep -rn "NEEDS_HUMAN_<KIND>" packs/ --include=*.mjs | grep -v test
```

Two semantics decide how a park behaves, and both live in canon:

- `isBlockingPark` (`queue/work-item.mjs`) — the kinds that **hold a task's lane**. Any other kind
  lets the generator file a fresh occurrence at the next anchor, which is where duplicate lanes
  come from.
- `SUPERSEDABLE_PARKS` (`queue/janitor-rules.mjs`) — the kinds a later clean run can **clear
  automatically**. A park outside that set is permanent until a human touches it.

A kind that is in neither set is a trap: it accumulates and it never drains. Check whether the
kind dominating your data is one, and say so plainly if it is.

### Discriminators that settle a cause

- **The janitor's own comment, verbatim.** Rule B (dead agent leash) reads *"carried
  `task:status:running-agent` for over 3h with no activity — the agent session that claimed it …
  never converged it"*; older items say `task:agent` and *"Labeling `needs-human`"*. Finding that
  text ends the question.
- **An execution record** — a `claudinite-task-exec v1 <pack>/<task> [#n] <status>` comment — means
  an **agent** converged the item deliberately. That park is genuine whatever else it looks like.
- **Timestamp clustering.** Many items across many repos moving within a minute or two is a
  scheduled sweep (each member's own janitor on a shared cron), never agent work. Scattered
  timestamps are per-repo runs. This separates two cohorts cheaply, before you read a single
  comment.
- **A result comment followed by a machine park** is the important sub-case: the agent *did the
  work*, posted its findings, and never closed the lane. That is a convergence failure, not a
  failed run, and it should never be reported as the same thing as a session that genuinely died.
- **A repeated park across repos in one window** is usually **one** condition, not N — check
  whether the threads name the same blocker before reporting a count.

### Reading comments without blowing the cap

`mcp__github__issue_read` with `method: "get_comments"` and `perPage: 8`–`10`. On an overflow,
parse the saved `tool-results/*.txt` with a small python slice rather than re-fetching:
`get_comments` returns a bare list; the search tools return GitHub's
`{total_count, incomplete_results, items}` envelope.

The park-setting comment is the **last** one, so when an item is long, page to the end rather than
reading from the start.

## 5. Report

Lead with the totals and the split, then the cause table, then the deep dive on whatever the run
found most interesting. State the fleet-wide mechanism where there is one — *why* these items
accumulated beats any per-item enumeration.

Deliver the complete per-repo listing as a **file**, grouped repo by repo with status and label
generation per row, so the conversation carries the analysis and the file carries the evidence.

Where a previous run's finding is corrected, **say so plainly and give the evidence that
overturned it.** A triage series that never revises itself is not being sampled.

Close with what is still open and what acting on it would take — as a recommendation. The relabel,
the close, the re-queue are all somebody's explicit call, and this skill does not make it.

input.body:
Today's fleet survey — 365 open issues across the 16-repo fleet, 162 of them queue items — was assembled by hand: sixteen `list_issues` calls transcribed into a TSV, a throwaway classifier, and a sampling pass to attribute causes. The analysis was worth having; none of the method survived the session. This lands it.

## What the skill carries

**Collection that survives the token cap** — the roster from `list_repos` minus archived repos and the fleet's `exclude` key, then one `list_issues` per repo with `fields: ["number","title","labels","updated_at"]`. Omitting `body` is what keeps a 99-issue repo readable. It routes explicitly around `search_issues` for enumeration, which this repo's RULES.md already records as untrustworthy for filtering.

**A suggested categorisation the run is told to go beyond** — park kind, label generation, lane duplication, non-park queue states, cross-repo duplicates, and the plain-issue label classes. Stated as a starting point, with the instruction that a run reproducing only these axes has under-delivered.

**Cause attribution, derived fresh rather than cached** — the skill tells the run to re-derive the park writers from canon each time, because the vocabulary is under active change. What it does fix are the two semantics that decide how a park behaves (`isBlockingPark`, `SUPERSEDABLE_PARKS`) and the discriminators that settle a cause from evidence: the janitor's verbatim leash comment, an agent's `claudinite-task-exec` record, and timestamp clustering as the cheap separator between a scheduled sweep and scattered agent work.

**The rule the run paid for.** A structural argument is a hypothesis until sampled. This session proved from canon that no agent could write a `decision` park — correct about `converge-item.mjs`, and still wrong, because agents replicate that transition by hand over MCP. One sampled comment thread overturned it, and the corrected split was 88 machine mislabels to 5 genuine parks.

Assessment only: the skill reports, and never relabels, closes, or re-queues.

## Second commit

`pack-badge-row` was already advisory on `main` — `claudinite-tasks` was added without the README row being re-derived, and it turns blocking on 2026-09-13. Second commit is the output of `converge-wiring --badges`, not a hand edit. `check_the_world` is clean on the branch.

Closes #393

## What the skill does with the freedom you asked for

The categorisation is deliberately **suggested, not prescribed**. It lists the axes this run found useful — park kind, label generation, lane duplication, non-park queue states, cross-repo duplicates, plain-issue classes — and then tells the run that reproducing only those has under-delivered, with a second list of cuts to try when the data suggests them (park age, whether an open PR is attached, task and repo concentration). The intent is a fresh read each time, not a recurring template.

The same applies to cause attribution, which is the part most likely to rot: the park vocabulary is under active change right now, so rather than freezing the writer table I found today, the skill hands the run the grep to re-derive it from canon. What it *does* fix are the two things that decide how a park behaves — `isBlockingPark` and `SUPERSEDABLE_PARKS` — plus the named trap of a kind in neither set, which is precisely the `decision` failure mode.

## The three techniques worth keeping

**Timestamp clustering** turned out to be the cheapest discriminator in the whole run — twenty items moving across nine repos inside forty seconds is a scheduled sweep, and that separated two cohorts before I read a single comment thread.

**A result comment followed by a machine park** is the sub-case I'd have missed without sampling: the agent did the work and posted its findings, then the leash parked it anyway. That is a convergence failure, not a failed run, and the skill says not to report them as the same thing.

**The sampling rule is the skill's spine**, and I wrote it against my own error rather than as generic caution — the `decision` argument was correct about `converge-item.mjs` and still wrong, and the corrected split (88 mislabels, 5 genuine) only emerged because one thread got read.

One judgement call worth flagging: I did **not** add a `VERSIONS.md` row.
